817: The landraces likewise differed significantly, the varietal effect being highly significant. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value, 2.051, followed by Kalojira with 1.627 and Radhunipagal with 1.626. Kalojira and Radhunipagal shared a common letter and were thus on par with each other, while Gobindabhog exceeded Radhunipagal by 0.426.
819: Storage period altered the L/B ratio significantly at the 1% level. In order of sampling, the values were 1.789 in fresh paddy, 1.785 at 4 months, 1.753 at 8 months and 1.746 at 12 months, the maximum occurring in fresh paddy and the minimum at 12 months. The value declined by 2.4% over the year.
821: Location and variety did not operate independently, their interaction being highly significant. Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman constituted the superior combination with 2.113, and Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman the inferior one with 1.170. Varietal ranking was not conserved across the three districts: Nadia yielded the order Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal, Kalojira; Purba Bardhaman the order Gobindabhog, Kalojira, Radhunipagal; and Birbhum/Howrah the order Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal, Kalojira. Such rank reversal establishes that the three environments did not act uniformly upon every landrace.
822: The location × storage interaction was highly significant. The highest mean, 1.882, was recorded for Nadia at 4 months and the lowest, 1.549, for Purba Bardhaman at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to +1.6% at Nadia, -8.6% at Purba Bardhaman and -0.3% at Birbhum/Howrah, a spread of 10.2 percentage points, with grain from Purba Bardhaman changing most and that from Nadia least. The rate of change during storage was therefore not uniform across grain of the three provenances.
823: The variety × storage interaction was highly significant. The highest mean, 2.114, was recorded for Gobindabhog at 8 months and the lowest, 1.547, for Radhunipagal at 8 months. Over twelve months the change amounted to +0.3% in Gobindabhog, -7.4% in Radhunipagal and -0.3% in Kalojira, Radhunipagal shifting furthest and Gobindabhog least. The three landraces consequently did not gain or lose at equivalent rates during storage.
824: The three-factor interaction attained the 1% level. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 2.177 was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months, and the minimum of 0.991 by Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months, a spread of 1.186. No single factor in isolation generated a range of this width; location, landrace and storage acted in combination, and the optimum outcome was attainable only through the appropriate conjunction of all three.
833: The L/B ratio, defined as grain length divided by grain breadth, characterises grain shape and determines the market class to which a rice is assigned. Birbhum and Howrah yielded the most slender grain at 1.865 and Purba Bardhaman the boldest at 1.607, with Nadia intermediate at 1.832. Where grain filling is curtailed by heat or water stress, the grain fails to attain its full length and the ratio declines accordingly. All three landraces fell well below the ratio of 2.5 to 3.0 that Kaul (1970) associated with long slender Basmati grain, which corroborates the classification of the aromatic rices of West Bengal within the small- and medium-grained group described by Singh et al. (2000). As the grain desiccates it contracts more along its length than across its breadth, and the ratio consequently falls; this shift registers as significant here only because the experimental error was exceptionally low.
837: Location exerted a highly significant effect on moisture. The highest value, 13.34%, was recorded at Nadia, followed by Birbhum/Howrah with 13.28% and Purba Bardhaman with 13.18%. No two locations shared a letter group, each therefore standing apart from the remaining two, with 0.16 percentage points separating the extremes.
839: The three landraces likewise differed, the varietal effect being highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 13.78%, followed by Gobindabhog with 13.38% and Radhunipagal with 12.64%. The three landraces resolved into discrete groups, Kalojira exceeding Radhunipagal by 1.14 percentage points.
841: Storage period altered moisture significantly at the 1% level. In order of sampling, the values were 13.29% in fresh paddy, 12.74% at 4 months, 13.95% at 8 months and 13.10% at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 8 months and the minimum at 4 months. A decline of 1.4% was registered over the full year.
843: The location × variety interaction was highly significant. Kalojira at Nadia constituted the superior combination with 13.91%, and Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman the inferior one with 12.58%. An identical varietal sequence (Kalojira first, Gobindabhog second and Radhunipagal third) obtained at all three sites; the interaction therefore modified the magnitude of the varietal differences while leaving their direction intact.
844: The location × storage interaction attained the 1% level. The highest mean, 14.14%, was recorded for Nadia at 8 months and the lowest, 12.68%, for Nadia at 4 months. Over 12 months of storage the change amounted to -1.6% at Nadia, -1.1% at Purba Bardhaman and -1.4% at Birbhum/Howrah. The magnitude of change scarcely differed between locations, storage having elicited an equivalent response in grain of all three provenances.
845: The variety × storage interaction attained the 1% level. The highest mean, 14.45%, was recorded for Kalojira at 8 months and the lowest, 12.21%, for Radhunipagal at 4 months. The twelve-month change amounted to -2.1% in Gobindabhog, -0.9% in Radhunipagal and -1.1% in Kalojira. None of the three shifted appreciably more than the others, and no differential response to storage was detected among them.
846: The three factors interacted significantly. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 14.80% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled at 8 months, and the minimum of 12.00% by Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 4 months, a spread of 2.80 percentage points. No single factor generated a range of comparable width; the effect proceeded from the three factors in conjunction, and all three required appropriate specification to secure the optimum outcome.
855: Moisture content determines whether stored paddy remains safe. Grain held at excessive moisture attracts insects and moulds, whereas over-dried grain shatters on handling. As all lots were dried and stored together at Mohanpur, the proximity of the values confirms that the lots attained comparable equilibrium within the common storage environment, indicating that the differences observed in the remaining traits are unlikely to be attributable to differential moisture retention between lots. Genkawa et al. (2008) demonstrated that brown rice held under ambient conditions continues to exchange moisture with the surrounding air, implying that this dynamic balance, rather than the initial moisture content of the grain, is the operative variable. Müller et al. (2022) accordingly recommend maintaining stored grain between 11 and 15% moisture, while Duangkhamchan et al. (2024) demonstrated in small farm barns in Thailand that moisture is seldom uniformly distributed through a stored lot, such that portions of a heap may exceed the safe threshold even where the mean appears acceptable.
860: Location exerted a highly significant effect on the aroma score. The highest value, 2.232, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Nadia with 2.228 and Purba Bardhaman with 2.127. Birbhum/Howrah and Nadia shared a common letter group, the difference between them being too small to be regarded as real, while the gap between the superior and inferior locations amounted to 0.104.
862: The three landraces also differed among themselves, the varietal effect being highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 2.506, followed by Gobindabhog with 2.083 and Radhunipagal with 1.998. Each landrace occupied a discrete letter group, Kalojira exceeding Radhunipagal by 0.508.
864: Storage period altered the aroma score to a highly significant degree. In order of sampling, the values were 2.605 in fresh paddy, 2.326 at 4 months, 2.071 at 8 months and 1.780 at 12 months, the peak occurring in fresh paddy and the trough at 12 months. By the close of the year the value had declined by 31.7%.
866: The location × variety interaction was significant at the 1% level. Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah constituted the superior combination with 2.561, and Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman the inferior one with 1.962. The varietal rank order (Kalojira first, Gobindabhog second, Radhunipagal third) held at every location; only the width of the varietal difference shifted, its direction remaining unaffected.
867: Location and storage period acted jointly. The highest mean, 2.646, was recorded for Nadia in fresh paddy and the lowest, 1.702, for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. Between harvest and 12 months the change amounted to -31.1% at Nadia, -32.9% at Purba Bardhaman and -31.0% at Birbhum/Howrah. The magnitude of change was comparable across locations, storage having been conducted at a single site and having acted uniformly on grain of every provenance.
868: Variety and storage period did not act independently. The highest mean, 2.908, was recorded for Kalojira in fresh paddy and the lowest, 1.615, for Radhunipagal at 12 months. Over the year Gobindabhog changed by -31.8%, Radhunipagal by -32.8% and Kalojira by -30.7%, Radhunipagal shifting furthest and Kalojira least. The three landraces therefore did not gain or lose at equivalent rates during storage.
869: The L × V × S interaction was highly significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 2.953 was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled as fresh paddy, and the minimum of 1.538 by Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months, a spread of 1.415. This range substantially exceeded that attributable to any individual factor; all three factors operated jointly, and the optimum outcome was contingent upon the correct specification of each.
878: Aroma constitutes the attribute conferring premium value upon these landraces, and its attrition removes the basis of that premium. Itani et al. (2004) ascribed such locational differences to temperature during ripening, and subsequent work has related them to the availability of proline and allied precursors in the filling grain. Kim et al. (2023) reported a corresponding pattern for overall sensory quality and observed that it declined more gradually than germination rate, which suggests that grain may forfeit a substantial proportion of its eating quality before any outward indication of deterioration becomes manifest. The appropriate storage period for aromatic rice therefore represents a compromise between milling quality and eating quality. Jie et al. (2024) determined that 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline in the aromatic cultivar Daohuaxiang declined by 43.9% within three months of conventional storage, as against 25.7% under a 35% carbon dioxide atmosphere, and attributed the loss to the concomitant rise in malondialdehyde and other markers of oxidative stress in the grain.
883: Location exerted a significant effect on total starch. The highest value, 72.97%, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Nadia with 72.69% and Purba Bardhaman with 72.35%. Birbhum/Howrah and Nadia shared a common letter group, the difference between them being too small to be regarded as real, while the superior and inferior locations differed by 0.62 percentage points.
885: The three landraces also differed among themselves, the varietal effect being highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 77.72%, followed by Gobindabhog with 72.19% and Radhunipagal with 68.10%. Each landrace occupied a discrete letter group, Kalojira exceeding Radhunipagal by 9.61 percentage points.
887: Storage period altered total starch to a highly significant degree. In order of sampling, the values were 73.36% in fresh paddy, 73.84% at 4 months, 71.81% at 8 months and 71.66% at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 4 months and the minimum at 12 months. Across the twelve months the value declined by 2.3%.
889: The location × variety interaction was highly significant. Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah constituted the superior combination with 78.07%, and Radhunipagal at Nadia the inferior one with 67.37%. The three landraces retained an identical order, Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal, at each location; the interaction therefore modified the magnitude of the varietal differences rather than their direction.
890: The location × storage interaction was significant. The highest mean, 74.96%, was recorded for Birbhum/Howrah at 4 months and the lowest, 71.25%, for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. By 12 months the three districts had changed by -1.9%, -3.1% and -2.0% respectively. All three locations shifted by closely comparable margins, the effect of storage proving independent of the district of origin.
891: Variety and storage did not interact significantly. The highest mean, 79.07%, was recorded for Kalojira at 4 months and the lowest, 66.95%, for Radhunipagal at 12 months. Twelve months of storage yielded changes of -2.9% in Gobindabhog, -2.5% in Radhunipagal and -1.6% in Kalojira. The three landraces shifted by nearly equivalent margins, storage having affected them comparably.
